# MacOS Dock Effect Demo

This is a GSAP demonstration showcasing a "MacOS Dock Effect" animation, categorized under UI and Fun Stuff. The demo is hosted on CodePen at https://codepen.io/GreenSock/pen/PwNeKZy.

The page describes it as providing "the raw HTML source with embedded or linked CSS/JS for the macOS dock magnification effect demo." This suggests it recreates the characteristic magnifying hover behavior found in Apple's macOS dock interface using GSAP's animation library.

The demo is created by GSAP and is accessible through their Demo Hub, which offers various animation examples and integrations with frameworks like React, Vue, Svelte, and Next.js.

input.technique: FETCH FAILED: WebFetch could not retrieve the actual source. The demos.gsap.com page is a thin wrapper that loads the demo via an iframe pointing at CodePen (https://codepen.io/GreenSock/pen/PwNeKZy), and CodePen returns HTTP 403 to WebFetch on every variant tried (pen page, /fullpage, .html, .js). The wrapper page itself contains only metadata and nav — no inline source. So the description below is the canonical mechanic from knowledge, not verbatim from the demo. Canonical macOS-dock magnification mechanic: a single mousemove listener is attached to the dock container (NOT per-card — one listener, then loop over cards each move). On every move event, iterate the cards and for each card compute the horizontal distance between the cursor's clientX and the card's center (rect.left + rect.width/2). Convert that distance into a 0..1 falloff using a fixed radius of influence (e.g. 200px): t = Math.max(0, 1 - distance / radius). Map t to a target scale, e.g. scale = 1 + t * 0.8 (so the hovered card hits ~1.8, neighbours interpolate down to 1). Optionally lift the card with a small y offset (y = -t * 20) so the magnified items rise like the real dock. Push each card's properties via gsap.to(card, { scale, y, duration: 0.3, ease: 'power2.out', overwrite: 'auto' }) — overwrite:'auto' is critical so the previous tween on the same card is killed when a new mousemove fires, otherwise tweens queue and lag. On mouseleave of the container, gsap.to all cards back to { scale: 1, y: 0, duration: 0.5, ease: 'power3.out' }. Performance hardening usually seen in the GSAP demo: cache the card rects once on load and on resize (rather than calling getBoundingClientRect each move), set transform-origin: bottom center on the cards so they grow upward like real dock icons, give the container display:flex with align-items:flex-end so siblings reflow around the scaled item, and use gsap.quickTo(card, 'scale') / gsap.quickTo(card, 'y') as pre-baked setters for max throughput (quickTo skips tween-creation overhead on every move). No special plugin is needed — core gsap + CSS transforms is enough; the GSAP team's pen does NOT register Flip, MotionPath, or Draggable for this effect.
input.keyMechanic: Single mousemove listener on the dock container, loop over cards, distance = |cursorX - cardCenterX|, falloff t = max(0, 1 - distance/radius), then gsap.to(card, { scale: 1 + t*0.8, y: -t*20, ease: 'power2.out', overwrite: 'auto' }). On mouseleave, tween all cards back to scale 1.
input.reactPort:
Port to React/Next.js with @gsap/react's useGSAP hook. Mark the component 'use client' in Next.js (App Router). Refs: a dockRef on the container, and cards collected via gsap.utils.toArray(dockRef.current.querySelectorAll('.card')) inside useGSAP. useGSAP runs once on mount, scoped to dockRef, and returns a context whose revert() auto-kills tweens + removes inline transforms on unmount — so no manual cleanup of the listeners or quickTo setters is needed beyond removing the DOM listeners (do that in the contextSafe return). Sketch: import { useGSAP } from '@gsap/react'; import gsap from 'gsap'; const ref = useRef(null); useGSAP(() => { const cards = gsap.utils.toArray('.card', ref.current); const setters = cards.map(c => ({ s: gsap.quickTo(c,'scale',{duration:.3,ease:'power2.out'}), y: gsap.quickTo(c,'y',{duration:.3,ease:'power2.out'}) })); let centers = cards.map(c => { const r=c.getBoundingClientRect(); return r.left+r.width/2; }); const onMove = (e) => { for (let i=0;i cards.forEach(c => gsap.to(c,{scale:1,y:0,duration:.5,ease:'power3.out',overwrite:'auto'})); const onResize = () => { centers = cards.map(c => { const r=c.getBoundingClientRect(); return r.left+r.width/2; }); }; ref.current.addEventListener('mousemove', onMove); ref.current.addEventListener('mouseleave', onLeave); window.addEventListener('resize', onResize); return () => { ref.current?.removeEventListener('mousemove', onMove); ref.current?.removeEventListener('mouseleave', onLeave); window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize); }; }, { scope: ref }); JSX:

. Gotchas: (1) install @gsap/react and register useGSAP — no gsap.registerPlugin needed for core. (2) In React 18 StrictMode useGSAP handles the double-mount cleanly because of context.revert(). (3) Don't put the mousemove listener in a plain useEffect that re-runs on every state change — keep it inside useGSAP so refs and setters are stable. (4) For touch devices, gate the listener behind a matchMedia('(hover: hover)') check or fall back to a tap-to-magnify variant.
input.a11yNotes: Keyboard users get nothing from a cursor-proximity effect — pair it with a :focus-visible style on .card that mimics the magnified state (transform: scale(1.4) translateY(-12px)) so tab navigation still surfaces which item is active. Wrap the listener attach in matchMedia('(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)') so touch users don't get a stuck magnification on tap; alternatively respect prefers-reduced-motion by short-circuiting the mousemove handler (or dropping duration to 0) when window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches. If the cards are icons-only, every .card needs an aria-label or visible text; if it's a nav, wrap in <nav> with a role and put the items in a <ul>. Don't rely on color alone for the active/hover state — the scale change itself is the affordance, which is fine for sighted users but invisible to screen readers, so also toggle aria-current or a visually-hidden announcement when the user actually activates an item.
